vignette:
Minh Tran is a 46-year-old Vietnamese American software engineer who lives with his wife in a quiet suburb outside of Houston. He was referred for psychological assessment following a request from his primary care physician, whom Minh had finally visited after months of his wife's gentle insistence. His PCL-5 score of 72 places him in a range indicative of severe posttraumatic stress, and the clinical picture that emerged across the intake and initial sessions is one of a man quietly dismantling his own life in the effort to feel safe inside it.

Minh served as a translator and tactical liaison embedded with a U.S. infantry unit during a combat deployment in Southeast Asia in his late twenties, a period he describes in fragments and then falls silent. What he has disclosed, haltingly and with long pauses, concerns a patrol ambush in which his unit came under sustained fire in a narrow jungle corridor. The attack began without warning - the first signal was the sound of a motorcycle engine idling somewhere beyond the tree line, used by the insurgents to communicate position, and then the world collapsed into smoke, burning fuel, and the smell of blood and scorched vegetation. Several men were killed in the minutes that followed. Minh survived by lying beneath a fallen colleague for what he believes was close to an hour. He has never been able to describe the full sequence of events in language. When asked directly, he gestures at the air, his hands moving as though tracing something that has no shape yet, and says only that it does not come to him in words. What comes to him instead is something closer to a loop - images and sounds that replay with a completeness and involuntary quality that he likens, unprompted, to a film he cannot switch off. He hears things in those replays: the motorcycle engine, voices, sounds he does not name.

In the years after his return to the United States, Minh built a career and a marriage, and for a long time the distance between his current life and that corridor felt sufficient. Then, roughly three years ago, a neighbor began storing a motorcycle in the driveway next door. The sound of the engine starting in the morning - ordinary, suburban, brief - began arriving inside Minh's body before he had any conscious awareness of it. He stopped being able to say exactly when the replays became more frequent, only that they did. He also cannot identify precisely when he began to notice smells differently: diesel exhaust, certain burning smells from the kitchen, the particular iron-tinged air before a Houston rainstorm. His wife has observed that he sometimes freezes mid-sentence and does not come back for several minutes.

What Minh has done in response, across the past two years in particular, is steadily reduce the perimeter of his life. He no longer goes to the gym, though he had been a consistent runner for over a decade. He stopped watching television with his wife in the evenings, citing a vague discomfort he could not explain, and he has not opened a news application on his phone in eighteen months. He avoids unfamiliar neighborhoods and declines work travel, telling colleagues his schedule does not permit it. He had come to believe, with a certainty that felt entirely reasonable to him, that in a place he did not know he would have no way to read the danger before it arrived. Even at home he remains watchful - he sits with his back to walls, checks the locks more than once, and feels a specific unease when strangers approach him in the parking lot of his own office building, even when he can see they are simply walking to their cars. He is certain something in his bearing or his alertness is the only thing standing between ordinary life and catastrophe.

The consequence that finally moved his wife to insist on a referral was a company team-building event Minh declined to attend, an absence his manager noted formally. He had been showering when he heard the neighbor's motorcycle outside, and the combination of that sound with the physical vulnerability of being unclothed was more than he could manage. He sat on the bathroom floor for forty minutes. He told his wife it had been nothing. She did not believe him. What Minh most fears, sitting now in the intake room, is that there is no version of the event he will ever be able to put into language - and that without language, nothing can be changed.
